# When the Tip Screen Aims High

## Full Story
<<HOOK>>You plan to leave a small tip, but the screen shows much bigger choices.<</HOOK>>

Why does this matter? A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card payments in New York City taxis. The tip screen showed a few ready-made choices.

The menu changed when a taxi fare moved just below or just above $15. This let researchers compare very similar rides with different tip choices on the screen. People who saw higher choices gave more. The number on the screen became their starting point.

But there was a limit. When the suggested tips were too high, more people chose to leave no credit card tip. A high choice could bring in more money, but it could also push some people away.

A 2022 Rutgers policy report says high suggested tips can be a business choice to raise income. But many people now seem unhappy. In a 2026 Popmenu survey, almost eight in ten respondents said tipping had become silly. Forty-four percent said they were tipping less than the year before.

### Point One

**Tips Have Grown**
The Rutgers report says restaurant tips in the United States were about 10% to 15% in the early 1970s. By the late 1990s, they were about 20%. Today, some digital screens may show choices as high as 35%. The number that feels “normal” has moved up over time.

### Point Two

**A Choice Others Can See**
A cash tip jar can feel private. A digital screen may feel different because a worker can see the customer’s choice. The Rutgers report calls this “guilt tipping.” In the 2026 Popmenu survey, 59% of respondents said a digital request made them feel they had to leave a tip.

## In One Line
A high suggested tip can raise what people give, but asking for too much can make them say no.
